clue.text: No government could be so cunning, in any case

indicators.note: 'in any case' asks for one word to sit inside the word any, which acts as its case

parts.note: taken as written
arch means sly or cunning

explanation.surface: Someone argues that statelessness would be equally crafty whatever happened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in any case' reads as the everyday 'anyway', but it is the container instruction: the word any forms the case.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchy is the absence of any ruling authority, a society without a state.

clue.text: Produced thick head in plant in this garden

indicators.note: in places the first two pieces inside the plant

parts.note: the arum is a plant, the lily family's cuckoo-pint
bore, as a mother bore a child, means produced

indicators.note: the first letter of the word it picks from

parts.note: the head of the word thick is its first letter

explanation.surface: Something grew a fat flower-head on a plant here in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the produced word and the thick head inside the plant, splitting it after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An arboretum is a botanical garden devoted to trees.

clue.text: A copperhead snake moving sideways

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: moving the letters means shuffling them into a new order

parts.note: the head of copper is its first letter, C
taken as written, part of the letters to be shuffled

explanation.surface: A venomous American snake slides away crabwise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copperhead' looks like the venomous snake; split it as copper's head. 'moving' rearranges that letter with the snake into SKANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking askance is looking out of the corner of the eye, obliquely.

clue.text: Writer once truly holding leading position

indicators.note: one word holding another contains it

parts.note: certes is an archaic word for truly, so 'once' marks it as old
the van is the vanguard, the leading position

explanation.surface: A former author sincerely kept at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once' belongs to the wordplay: CERTES is old for 'truly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Miguel de Cervantes wrote Don Quixote.

clue.text: Ship's course set northward on lake

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading upward, so the word is reversed

parts.note: a way is a course or route
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A vessel's route heads north across a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set northward' turns WAY into YAW.
explanation.definitionFit: A yawl is a two-masted sailing boat.

clue.text: Leaders of king's enemies talk about bill in parliament

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first-letter group surrounds the next piece
the leaders of the words king's, enemies and talk are their opening letters

parts.note: a bill is a headland, as is a ness (Portland Bill, Dungeness)

explanation.surface: The king's foes' spokesmen debate a piece of legislation in the House.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts NESS inside KET, the leaders of king's, enemies and talk, after the K. 'bill' looks like legislation but is a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Knesset is the Israeli national legislature.

clue.text: Nothing in the work gets altered for this book

indicators.note: nothing sits in the jumbled group of letters
altered means the letters of the and work are rearranged

parts.note: nil means nothing

explanation.surface: A book has had none of its text changed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets altered' rearranges the clue's 'the work' into KEWORTH; 'in' then puts the word for nothing inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Kenilworth is a historical novel by Sir Walter Scott.

clue.text: Disease so terminal for wheat?

parts.note: ergo is Latin for therefore, so

indicators.note: the terminal of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Is this the illness that finishes off a wheat crop?
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that ergot mostly attacks rye, though it does strike wheat.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergot is a fungal blight of cereals such as rye.

clue.text: Celebrity has to perform in terribly smart location

indicators.note: the performing word goes inside the reworked letters
terribly signals that smart is mangled into a new order

parts.note: to do is to perform

explanation.surface: A star must put on a show in a dreadfully fashionable venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' rearranges the clue's 'smart' into STARM; 'in' puts the performing word inside it. 'location' only fills out the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Fame is the condition of being a big name, a star.

clue.text: Cantankerous jury's conclusion after trial

indicators.note: after places the final letter behind the trial word

parts.note: a test is a trial

indicators.note: the conclusion of jury is its last letter

explanation.surface: A grumpy juror's verdict follows a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trial' suggests a court case; here it is TEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Testy and cantankerous both mean irritable and quarrelsome.

clue.text: Bad break for unfortunate hunter

indicators.note: a bad break is a broken one, so the letters of the word break are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: An unlucky fracture or turn of fortune strikes a hunter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' rearranges BREAK. In Lewis Carroll's poem The Hunting of the Snark the Baker is the hunter who meets a Boojum and vanishes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Baker is the ill-fated member of the hunting party in Carroll's Snark poem.

clue.text: Vessel outside port

parts.note: a container that goes round a fortified wine such as port, rather than a ship outside a harbour

explanation.surface: A ship lies at anchor just beyond the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' and 'port' suggest shipping; read port as the drink and the vessel holds it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stemmed drinking glass is the vessel that surrounds a serving of port.

clue.text: Disheartened fugitive's flight starts here

indicators.note: losing its heart means the word loses its central letter

parts.note: a fugitive is a runaway

explanation.surface: A downcast escapee's getaway begins at this point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disheartened' takes the middle A out of RUNAWAY. 'flight' is an aircraft's flight, not the escape.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft begins its journey by taking off along the airstrip.

clue.text: Not before time, head departs in excellent spirits

indicators.note: the head of a word departing means its first letter goes

parts.note: belatedly means late, not before time

explanation.surface: At long last, the headmaster leaves in high good humour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head departs' removes the B from BELATEDLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with great joy or high spirits is the adverbial sense of being exultant.

clue.text: Part of Oxford's wine deposit for top people

parts.note: an Oxford is a style of lace-up shoe, and the upper is the part above the sole
crust is the deposit that forms in bottles of vintage port

explanation.surface: Some of Oxford's wine dregs are reserved for the elite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oxford' suggests the university; it is an Oxford shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper crust is a colloquial term for the aristocracy.

clue.text: Dickensian shop girl's flower

definitions.meaning: Little Nell ... of Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop
crossword 'flower' is something that flows, a river: here an English river through the Midlands

explanation.surface: A Dickens heroine's blossom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flower' means a river, a thing that flows; the Trent is one of England's main rivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Nell's surname in Dickens is Trent, and the Trent is a long Midlands river.

clue.text: Workers who control movements of shares

definitions.text: Workers who control movements of shares

parts.words: Workers who control movements of shares
parts.note: the shares are ploughshares, the blades steered by farm labourers, not stock market holdings

explanation.surface: Stockbrokers who manage trading in stocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shares' suggests the stock exchange; a share is also the cutting blade of a plough.
explanation.definitionFit: Farm labourers who guide a plough direct where its blades travel.

clue.text: Sponsor for film

definitions.meaning: a sponsor at a christening, a godparent

explanation.definitionFit: A man who stands sponsor at a baptism has this title, as does the famous gangster film.

clue.text: Officer is a relatively insensitive individual

definitions.meaning: naval slang for a first lieutenant
a ..., someone more lacking in feeling

explanation.surface: An officer is less sensitive than most.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first word as NUMB-ER: more numb, so less able to feel.
explanation.definitionFit: The first lieutenant on a ship is so called, and a more numb person is a 'numb-er' one.

clue.text: Check on financial position brings about trial

parts.note: to mean can be to cause or bring about
a test is a trial

explanation.surface: A credit check leads to a court case.
explanation.definitionFit: Benefit authorities assess income and savings with this inquiry before giving aid.

clue.text: For meat, for instance, tame a couple of animals

parts.note: a nag is an old horse
a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: Domesticate a pair of beasts for the meat supply.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: the word tame is a rearrangement of meat, so it stands for meat in this sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Tame is a jumble of meat's letters, the kind of letter-play this word names.

clue.text: Engineer current stoppage without union, in fact

indicators.note: without in the old sense of outside, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: a dam is an engineered barrier stopping a water current
TU is short for trade union

explanation.surface: An engineer halts the electric current without consulting the union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not 'lacking', so the union is placed within the barrier.
explanation.definitionFit: A datum is a single given piece of information.

clue.text: Drink with a colleague? Quite so!

parts.note: a tot is a small drink of spirits
an ally is a partner or colleague

explanation.surface: Have a drink with a workmate? Absolutely!
explanation.definitionFit: As an exclamation it means absolutely or I agree.

clue.text: Drill needed for dentist's work, for example

definitions.meaning: a professional's business, like a doctor's or dentist's surgery

explanation.surface: A dentist needs a drill to do the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drill' suggests the dentist's tool; it is repetitive exercise.
explanation.definitionFit: Rehearsal is repeated exercise, and a dental surgery is a professional's business.

clue.text: Rock-rabbit

definitions.meaning: the name comes from Greek petros, rock

explanation.definitionFit: The apostle's name means stone, and Beatrix Potter's rabbit has this name.

clue.text: Reliant on garage to provide shelter for this vehicle

indicators.note: the words shelter the answer, holding it within their letters

explanation.surface: A Reliant car depends on its garage to keep it under cover.
explanation.walkthrough: A Reliant is a British make of small car, a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonga is a light two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage used in India.

clue.text: Man cornered, to begin with, in fortress

definitions.meaning: a chess piece (man) that starts the game in a corner square

explanation.surface: A man is trapped in a stronghold from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is a chessman: the rook starts in a corner of the board.
explanation.definitionFit: The rook, also called by this name, begins in the board's corner; the word also means a fortified keep.

clue.text: Pack up the brandy

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: to cram is to pack tightly

explanation.surface: Put the bottle of brandy away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses CRAM.
explanation.definitionFit: Marc is a spirit distilled from grape pressings.

clue.text: Terrifying arachnid, initially encountered with natural distress

definitions.text: Terrifying arachnid, initially encountered with natural distress

indicators.note: initially means take the opening letters of the words Terrifying and arachnid
to distress something is to upset or disorder it, so the letters of natural are rearranged

explanation.surface: A frightening spider, met for the first time, naturally causes alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: TA, the first letters of Terrifying arachnid, then 'distress' rearranges NATURAL into RANTULA.
explanation.definitionFit: This large hairy spider is the arachnid most people find frightening.

clue.text: That chap will ring — what will you say?

parts.note: he'll is the short form of he will
O is shaped like a ring

explanation.surface: Someone will phone you, so what are you going to say?
explanation.walkthrough: 'ring' suggests the phone; here it is the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the usual greeting said on picking up the telephone.

clue.text: Defence side introduced by the beak

indicators.note: to be introduced by something is to be preceded by it, so that piece comes first

parts.note: a ram is the beak at the prow of a warship
a part is a side, as in taking someone's part

explanation.surface: A defence counsel's case is presented by the magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beak' is British slang for a magistrate, but here it is a warship's ram.
explanation.definitionFit: A rampart is a defensive earthen bank or wall round a fort.

clue.text: Historian heard but not seen in Northern town

indicators.note: a word heard but not seen is pronounced the same while written differently, as the S of the town is silent

parts.note: Carlisle is a city in Cumbria in northern England

explanation.surface: A historian is audible but invisible somewhere in the North.
explanation.walkthrough: Carlisle, the Cumbrian city near the Scottish border, is said 'car-LILE', its S silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Carlyle wrote The French Revolution and other histories.
